# Aperture

- Route: `/tools/aperture`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `photo`
- Slug: `aperture`

## Summary

A layer-based photo editor in your browser: exposure, curves, color, masks, healing and presets, exported at full resolution. (Photo editing)

## Details

Aperture is the photo editor inside Media Manipulator. It opens a single photo full screen, with no ads, and lets you build the edit as a stack of adjustment layers over the untouched original: an exposure layer, a curve, an HSL layer limited to one color range, a vignette, a sharpen pass, each with its own opacity, blend mode and optional mask. The preview is drawn on your graphics card from a 1920 px copy so every slider responds immediately, and the export is rendered on our server from the original file at full resolution with the same math. Nothing you do here rewrites the file you opened; the result is always a new file named after the original with the word retouched added.
### What it does
- Keeps every edit as a separate adjustment layer, up to 64 per photo, so any layer can be hidden, reordered, duplicated, re-tuned or deleted later without touching the rest of the stack.
- Covers global tone and color in the Basic, Curves, Levels, Color (HSL), Color balance, Black & white, Channel mixer, Photo filter, Split toning, LUT and Effects panels, with sliders whose ranges match a desktop editor.
- Limits any layer to part of the frame with a linear gradient, a radial, a painted brush, a luminosity range, a color range picked with an eyedropper, or an AI subject mask, combined by add, subtract or intersect.
- Repairs pixels with the Heal tool (paint the spots, press Heal, and an inpainting model fills them on our GPU), a Red-eye fix, and the Geometry panel for crop, straighten, rotate, flip and four-corner perspective.
- Saves and reapplies looks: 18 built-in presets plus Auto, your own presets stored in this browser or exported as JSON, and, once you are signed in on any plan, the same stack applied to a batch of other photos.
### How to use it
1. Open a photo: Drop a file on this page. The browser decodes it, the editor opens and the live histogram appears under the panels.
2. Stack adjustments: Move a slider in any panel and a layer appears in the Layers list. Give it a mask, lower its opacity, or switch it to the Luminosity or Color blend.
3. Compare and refine: Press and hold the backslash key to see the original, or use Split view for a side-by-side. Undo, redo and the History panel go back as far as you like.
4. Export at full size: Choose JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF or TIFF, a quality from 1 to 100, whether to keep metadata, and a size cap. The server renders the original and the file downloads.
### Supported formats
- Input: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF, BMP
- Output: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, TIFF
- HEIC, HEIF, TIFF and BMP need an account: the server decodes them into a preview copy because browsers do not. The other formats open locally.
- Approximate export sizes per megapixel shown in the dialog: JPG at quality 92 about 0.45 MB, WebP about 0.3 MB, AVIF about 0.2 MB, PNG about 2.5 MB for photos, TIFF about 3.0 MB.
### Technical details
- Working values are sRGB floats from 0 to 1 and every stage clamps to that range; only the Exposure and White balance layers convert to linear light first (sRGB decode: v / 12.92 below 0.04045, else ((v + 0.055) / 1.055) to the power 2.4) and encode back afterwards.
- Layers apply in stack order, bottom to top. Each one computes its adjusted color, then the blend mode takes the whole result (Normal), only the BT.709 luma shift with weights 0.2126, 0.7152 and 0.0722 (Luminosity) or only the chroma shift (Color), and finally the layer opacity times the mask value, 0 to 1, mixes it with the input.
- The preview is drawn on your GPU in WebGL2 from a 1920 px copy of the photo; the exported file is rendered on our server from the original at full resolution with the same formulas, and the two agree within a small documented tolerance: color operations differ by a mean of at most one 8-bit level and never more than four, convolutions by at most eight, and grain is exact because both sides share one hash.
- A mask is folded from its components in order, starting from 0: Add takes the larger of the running value and the component, Subtract takes the smaller of the running value and one minus the component, Intersect takes the smaller of the two. Mask feather is a Gaussian blur whose sigma is the feather percentage times 0.05 times the longer image side; invert and mask strength apply after the blur.
- Geometry is one inverse mapping: rotation, straighten angle, flip, the four-corner perspective quad and the crop are composed into a single transform, and output pixels are sampled bilinearly from the source, so stacking several geometry changes does not resample the photo more than once.
- Images up to 4 megapixels are rendered on the server in float64 to match the TypeScript reference bit for bit; larger ones use float32. The selftest that runs at deploy compares 126 golden renders and currently measures a maximum error of one 8-bit level.
### When not to use it
Aperture edits one photo at a time with parametric layers, so it is the wrong tool for pixel painting, text and shape overlays, compositing two photos, or drawing. If you only need a smaller file, the image compressor does that in one step without opening an editor; if you need a transparent cutout, the background remover returns a PNG directly; and if you want to strip location data before posting, the EXIF remover is quicker than exporting with metadata set to Strip. Batch edits of more than 25 photos are also outside its limits.
### Use cases
- Rescue a phone photo: Lift the shadows, pull back a blown sky with a gradient-masked Exposure layer, warm the white balance, and export a 12 MP JPG without installing anything.
- Product shots for a listing: Straighten, crop to 1:1 or 4:5, set a clean white balance with the eyedropper, heal dust, sharpen with a radius of 1 px and apply the same stack to the other 9 shots in the batch.
- A consistent look across a set: Build the look once, save it as a preset, and reapply it. The preset adds its layers as a group so you can still adjust the exposure per photo underneath it.
- Portraits and skin: Heal blemishes, soften with Clarity at -20 under a brush mask, lower Reds saturation in HSL by a few points, and keep the eyes sharp with a radial mask on a Sharpen layer.
### FAQ
Q: Is Aperture a destructive editor?
A: No. The original file is never modified. Every change is a parameter on a layer, the stack is stored as a small JSON document next to the photo, and the export writes a new file named with retouched before the extension.
Q: How many layers and masks can one photo have?
A: Up to 64 adjustment layers, each with its own opacity from 0 to 100 percent, a Normal, Luminosity or Color blend, and an optional mask built from any number of gradient, radial, brush, luminosity, color-range or subject components.
Q: What is the largest photo I can export?
A: Daily limits and file caps depend on the plan; quote them only from the live plan block.
Q: Which operations count against my daily allowance?
A: Each export is one everyday operation, the first Select subject on a given photo is one everyday operation (an identical repeat is a free cache hit), and each press of Heal is one AI operation. Sliders, undo, presets and the other five mask kinds cost nothing. The exact daily numbers are on the pricing page.
Q: Can I open HEIC photos from an iPhone?
A: Yes when you are signed in. The browser cannot decode HEIC, HEIF, TIFF or BMP on its own, so the server makes a preview copy for the editor; JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF and AVIF open directly without an account.
Q: Will the exported photo look exactly like the preview?
A: Within a documented tolerance. Color adjustments match to within a few 8-bit levels at worst and are usually identical; grain is bit-identical. The preview is computed from a 1920 px copy, so very fine sharpening or noise reduction can look slightly different at full size, which is why the export is treated as ground truth.
